w: Built by Emperor Tiberius and completed in AD 27, Villa Jovis is the largest of the twelve Tiberian villas on Capri, and the emperor ruled from here until his death in AD 37. The complex climbs several terraces across a 40-metre change in elevation and covers some 7,000 square metres.
s: Tiberius ruled Rome from this clifftop palace
_facts: Built by Tiberius, completed AD 27
Largest of 12 Tiberian villas on Capri (per Tacitus)
Tiberius ruled from here until his death in AD 37
Covers about 7,000 sq m across multiple terraces, 40m elevation change

w: Standing on the headland it is named for, about 3 km southwest of Anacapri, the Faro di Punta Carena has guided ships along Capri's coast since 1867. Construction on the lighthouse began five years earlier, in 1862, and it remains an active aid to navigation on the island's exposed southwestern point today.
s: Working lighthouse on Capri's wild southwest tip
_facts: Located about 3km southwest of Anacapri
Active lighthouse since 1867
Construction began in 1862

w: Its name means 'here one heals' in Italian: the Quisisana began in 1845 as a sanatorium founded by British doctor George Sidney Clark, who turned it into a grand hotel in 1861. Guests since have included Oscar Wilde, Maxim Gorky and King Farouk I during his exile. Now Capri's largest hotel, 148 rooms.
s: Sanatorium turned grand hotel; an exiled king once stayed
_facts: Founded 1845 as a sanatorium by Dr. George Sidney Clark
Became a grand hotel in 1861; name means 'here one heals'
Guests included Oscar Wilde, Gorky, Sartre, King Farouk in exile
Capri's largest hotel, 148 rooms

w: Built in 1719 on Anacapri's Piazza San Nicola, this octagonal Baroque church is best known for what lies underfoot: a notable majolica floor mosaic that earned it a monument designation. The Roman Catholic church's distinctive eight-sided plan sets it apart from Capri's other village churches.
s: Octagonal Baroque church with a majolica floor
_facts: Built 1719, Piazza San Nicola, Anacapri
Octagonal Baroque design
Notable majolica floor mosaic; monument-designated

w: Known in Italian as the Grotta Azzurra, this sea cave glows electric blue when sunlight passes through an underwater cavity and reflects back up through the water. It reaches about 50 metres into the cliff at the surface and drops to roughly 150 metres deep over a sandy floor.
s: Sea cave that glows electric blue underwater
_facts: Italian name: Grotta Azzurra
Blue glow from sunlight refracted through an underwater opening
Extends about 50m into the cliff, roughly 150m deep, sandy bottom

w: At 589 metres, Monte Solaro is Capri's highest point, its sheer dolomitic slopes forming an 'unsurpassable partition' between the island's east and west. The 'Fortino di Bruto' blockhouse near the summit saw use in early-19th-century Britain-France battles, and a statue of Augustus now stands at the top.
s: Capri's highest peak, with a British-era blockhouse
_facts: Elevation 589m, Capri's highest point
Fortino di Bruto blockhouse used in early-19th-century Britain-France battles
Statue of Augustus, first to land on Capri, stands at the summit
Popular with painters for its views

w: Founded in 1363 by Giacomo Arcucci, this Carthusian charterhouse holds a pharmacy and women's church, the monks' quarters, and guest buildings. Its Great Cloister is late Renaissance, while the Small Cloister still carries Roman marble columns. No longer a monastery, it is now a museum and cultural venue.
s: 14th-century charterhouse with Roman marble cloisters
_facts: Founded 1363 by Giacomo Arcucci
Carthusian charterhouse (monastery)
Small Cloister has Roman marble columns; Great Cloister is late Renaissance
Now a museum and event venue

w: The 'Fern Grotto' sits about 200 metres above the sea on Capri's southern side, one of the island's oldest inhabited spots. Excavations begun in 1882 by Ignazio Cerio turned up 549 finds and fossils in its 370-square-metre chamber, many dated to the Neolithic period.
s: Fern Grotto with Neolithic finds, 200m above the sea
_facts: About 200m above sea level, southern Capri
Excavated since 1882 by Ignazio Cerio
549 finds/fossils recovered, many Neolithic
Finds held at Centro Caprense and University of Naples museums

w: On the outskirts of Anacapri, this park was founded in 2000 by Swedish professor Gunnar Adler-Karlsson and his wife Marianne Ehrnford as an open-air gallery of ideas: small tablets scattered through the grounds carry quotes from 60 different Western philosophers.
s: A park of philosopher quote-tablets above Anacapri
_facts: Parco Filosofico, founded 2000
Founded by Gunnar Adler-Karlsson and Marianne Ehrnford
Tablets bear quotes from 60 Western philosophers

w: Named for the patron saint of Capri, San Costanzo, this monumental church served as the cathedral of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Capri from 987 until 1560, when that role passed elsewhere. It remains one of the island's most historically significant religious buildings, tied to Capri's own patron saint.
s: Former cathedral named for Capri's patron saint
_facts: Named for San Costanzo, patron saint of Capri
Served as the Diocese of Capri's cathedral, 987-1560

n: Chiesa di Santa Maria di Costantinopoli
w: Built in the eleventh century in Anacapri's Li Curti district and restored in the seventeenth, this church blends Gothic and Byzantine features and holds several works by the Flemish painter Willem Borremans. Once Anacapri's parish church, it was later superseded in that role by the Chiesa di Santa Sofia.
s: 11th-century church with Gothic-Byzantine roots
_facts: Built 11th century, restored 17th century
Gothic and Byzantine architectural elements
Holds works by Flemish painter Willem Borremans
Former parish church of Anacapri, later replaced by Santa Sofia

w: Called 'Capri's most otherworldly church', this Franciscan hermitage on Monte Solaro's Cetrella slopes was built in the Middle Ages, its low-vaulted ceiling lined in stucco. Islanders once prayed here for their fishermen, and its venerated Madonna statue has drawn pilgrims, among them Rainer Maria Rilke.
s: Medieval hermitage where fishermen's families prayed
_facts: Franciscan chapel and hermitage, medieval origin
Located on Monte Solaro's Cetrella area
Venerated Madonna statue; pilgrims included Rainer Maria Rilke
Islanders prayed here for fishermen's safety

w: The 'Green Cave' is a sea cave on Capri's rugged, sirocco-battered coast, its light show a composite effect: blue light reflected up through the water plays against the cave's yellowish rock, reading as green. Best seen by boat on a calm day, in the lower inlet known as l'Assaggio Verde.
s: A sea cave that glows green instead of blue
_facts: Italian name: Grotta Verde
Green light from blue light reflecting off yellowish rock
Best visited by boat in calm conditions
Lower section known as l'Assaggio Verde

w: Founded in 1878 by Englishman George Hayward, Capri's non-Catholic cemetery holds 204 graves from 21 nations, mostly English, German, Russian and American, alongside Jews, Orthodox Christians and some Catholics. Notable burials include Baron Jacques d'Adelswaerd-Fersen, Gracie Fields and Norman Douglas.
s: Non-Catholic burial ground for Capri's foreign exiles
_facts: Founded 1878 by George Hayward
204 graves, 21 nationalities
Notable interments: Fersen, Gracie Fields, Norman Douglas, von Uexkuell
Restored by the municipality from 1986 after postwar neglect

w: Perched on the summit of Lo Capo hill within the Villa Jovis site, this chapel-like church was built around 1610 at the island's eastern extremity. It holds a bronze Madonna statue given in 1979 by painter Guido Odierna; in the late 19th century a hermit lived here, keeping a visitors' book and selling wine.
s: A hilltop chapel where a hermit once sold wine
_facts: Built around 1610, within the Villa Jovis site
Bronze Madonna statue, 1979 gift by Guido Odierna
Late-19th-century hermit kept a visitors' book, sold wine

w: On Capri's southwestern shore, this modest cave has yielded Impasto ware fragments from the Copper Age and artefacts of the Gaudo culture, also found at the nearby Grotta delle Felci. A quiet counterpart to Capri's better-known grottoes, it marks the island's prehistoric occupation.
s: A cave holding Copper Age pottery fragments
_facts: Copper Age Impasto ware fragments found here
Gaudo culture artifacts identified
Located on southwestern Capri

w: Also called the Palatium, this is one of the twelve villas of Tiberius on Capri, built by Augustus and later modified by his successor. Its terraces ran from the clifftop to the beach, with a semicircular nymphaeum; a Royal Geographical Society account called it Capri's most extensive Roman remains.
s: Augustus's seaside palace, later expanded by Tiberius
_facts: Built by Augustus, modified by Tiberius
One of 12 Tiberian villas on Capri
Includes a semicircular nymphaeum; excavated from 1932 by Amedeo Maiuri
Described as the most extensive Roman remains on Capri's coast

w: Built in 1378 by monks of the Certosa di San Giacomo to watch for Saracen raiders, this medieval tower on the road to Punta Carena was later converted into a villa. From 1908 to 1943 it was home to Swedish physician and writer Axel Munthe, who wrote his bestselling memoir The Story of San Michele while living here.
s: Medieval watchtower where Axel Munthe wrote his memoir
_facts: Built 1378 by Certosa di San Giacomo monks
Built to guard against Saracen incursions
Home to Axel Munthe 1908-1943
Munthe wrote The Story of San Michele here

w: Set along the Via Tragara, this house was once home to Camille du Locle before illustrator Jan Styka enlarged it in Italian Renaissance style. Edwin Cerio later requisitioned it, stripping those additions to return it to a mediterranean casa style; Jacques d'Adelswaerd-Fersen lived here before Villa Lysis was finished.
s: Via Tragara villa with a Renaissance-then-stripped past
_facts: Home of Camille du Locle, later enlarged by illustrator Jan Styka
Requisitioned by Edwin Cerio, who reverted it to casa mediterranea style
Jacques d'Adelswaerd-Fersen lived here before Villa Lysis was finished
Now a hotel with notable gardens

w: Built 1907-1910 by writer-engineer Edwin Cerio, this house overlooks the Faraglioni stacks, which Homer's Odyssey casts as boulders hurled by the Cyclops Polyphemus and Virgil's Aeneid makes the sirens' perch. Cerio filled it with lily-and-thistle ceramic floors and lines from the Song of Songs.
s: A villa overlooking the sirens' rocks of legend
_facts: Built 1907-1910 by Edwin Cerio
Overlooks the Faraglioni, linked to Homer's Cyclops and Virgil's sirens
Ceramic floors quote the Song of Songs
Visited by Futurism founder Filippo Tommaso Marinetti

w: Established in 1956 on land donated to the Swedish state by physician Axel Munthe, this bird observatory tracked Capri's spring migrations through annual ringing by Swedish researchers until 1983. Since 1986 it has been run jointly by Italian and Swedish teams.
s: Bird research station born from Axel Munthe's gift
_facts: Founded 1956 on land donated by Axel Munthe
Swedish researchers conducted spring bird ringing until 1983
Since 1986, run by joint Italian-Swedish teams
